item.title: x86 Architectural Registers
item.description:
x86 architectural registers hold programmer-visible integer, control, status, address-translation, debug, floating-point, and vector state. Width and availability depend on execution mode and enabled extensions. Calling conventions assign software roles to a subset of these registers but do not change their architectural behavior.

General-Purpose Registers and Subregisters #

IA-32 exposes EAX, EBX, ECX, EDX, ESI, EDI, EBP, and ESP. x86-64 widens them to RAX through RSP and adds R8 through R15. Subregisters name parts of the same architectural register:

item.title: x86 Memory Organization
item.description:
x86 memory organization developed in response to successive limits on register width, address-bus width, protection, and multitasking. Physical memory remains a byte-addressed space: after translation, the processor places a physical address on the memory interface. The path to that address, however, has changed substantially.

An x86 instruction first computes an effective address (EA), also called an offset. In modes with usable segmentation, a selected segment contributes a base, producing a linear address. With paging enabled, page tables translate the linear address to a physical address. The stages are therefore:

item.title: x86 Protected Mode and Privilege
item.description:
x86 protected mode combines descriptor-based segmentation, controlled control transfers, paging, and privileged instructions. Long mode reduces ordinary segmentation but retains descriptor tables, privilege levels, interrupt gates, and a task-state segment (TSS). Operating systems use those mechanisms to enter the kernel and isolate user execution, while page tables provide the primary memory-protection boundary on current x86-64 systems.

Table Registers #

The global descriptor table (GDT) contains code, data, and system descriptors shared by a logical processor. GDTR stores the GDT’s linear base and byte limit. GDT entry zero is conventionally a null descriptor, which makes a selector with index zero unusable for ordinary code or data access.

item.title: x86 and x86-64 Instruction Encoding
item.description:
x86 uses variable-length instructions. An instruction can contain legacy prefixes, an opcode, a ModR/M byte, a scale-index-base (SIB) byte, a displacement, and an immediate. Only the opcode is always present:

Long mode can add a REX prefix between the legacy prefixes and opcode. VEX, XOP, and EVEX encodings replace parts of this layout for newer instruction families. Regardless of the form, an architectural x86 instruction cannot exceed 15 bytes.

item.title: x86 Instruction Families
item.description:
x86 groups a large, irregular instruction set behind common data movement, arithmetic, bit manipulation, control-flow, and string-processing patterns. Operand size, address size, execution mode, prefixes, and ISA extensions can change an instruction’s encoding or availability. Intel’s and AMD’s architecture manuals remain authoritative; successful assembly only proves that a tool can encode the source.

Data Movement and Address Generation #

MOV copies an immediate or register value to a register or memory, or copies memory to a register. An ordinary MOV has at most one explicit memory operand. MOVZX zero-extends a narrower integer, while MOVSX and MOVSXD sign-extend. A 32-bit general-purpose-register destination in 64-bit mode implicitly clears the upper 32 bits.

item.title: x86 and x86-64 Architecture Overview
item.description:
x86 began with Intel’s 16-bit 8086. The 80286 introduced protected mode, IA-32 established the 32-bit programming model and paging, and AMD64 extended the architecture to 64-bit execution. Intel calls the combined architecture Intel 64 and IA-32; AMD documentation uses AMD64. Vendor names do not determine every feature, so software must discover extensions explicitly.
